question: to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Willemien Koning (PPE), Jeannette Baljeu (Renew), Rachel Blom (PfE) Subject:

Blockades in the Strait of Hormuz are causing global fuel shortages and kerosene is no exception. It is essential for passenger and cargo transport in the EU aviation sector that the remaining kerosene be used as efficiently as possible. However, under EU law, European airlines must operate at least 80 per cent of their flights in order not to lose landing rights. During the coronavirus pandemic, the Commission suspended this rule to prevent inefficient flights and so-called ghost flights. 1.

In view of the exceptional situation in the Middle East, the Commission’s call for fuel economy and the expected long recovery period, is the Commission prepared to temporarily suspend the EU Slot Allocation Regulation once again or to make it more flexible (for example, through an EU slot exemption from the 80-20 rule), so that airlines can use kerosene more efficiently to carry as many passengers and cargo as possible?

Is the Commission prepared to clarify the situation as to whether severe shortages and the high price of kerosene constitute grounds for ‘justified non-use of slots’, and how will harmonised application by slot coordinators be ensured in this regard?
What is the Commission’s take on a temporary suspension of the anti-tankering rules in the ReFuelEU Regulation, so that EU airlines can refuel more outside the EU if necessary?
answer: (English version) to the Commission Bert-Jan Ruissen (ECR), Willemien Koning (PPE), Jeannette Baljeu (Renew), Rachel Blom (PfE) (7 May 2026) Subject: Aviation fuel shortage Blockades in the Strait of Hormuz are causing global fuel shortages and kerosene is no exception. It is essential for passenger and cargo transport in the EU aviation sector that the remaining kerosene be used as efficiently as possible. However, under EU law, European airlines must operate at least 80% of their flights in order not to lose landing rights. During the coronavirus pandemic, the Commission suspended this rule to prevent inefficient flights and so-called ghost flights. 1. In view of the exceptional situation in the Middle East, the Commission’s call for fuel economy and the expected long recovery period, is the Commission prepared to temporarily suspend the EU Slot Allocation Regulation once again or to make it more flexible (for example, through an EU slot exemption from the 80-20 rule), so that airlines can use kerosene more efficiently to carry as many passengers and cargo as possible? 2. Is the Commission prepared to clarify the situation as to whether severe shortages and the high price of kerosene constitute grounds for ‘justified non-use of slots’, and how will harmonised application by slot coordinators be ensured in this regard? 3. What is the Commission’s take on a temporary suspension of the anti-tankering rules in the ReFuelEU Regulation, so that EU airlines can refuel more outside the EU if necessary? (15 June 2026) 1. Any suspension of the slot use rules must be underpinned by reliable data and targeted to the needs of the sector. While it is not excluded that disruptions could arise in certain areas, at present there is no immediate threat to the security of fuel supply. The Commission is committed to supporting the aviation sector amid continued uncertainty on the length and severity of the Middle East crisis, when and where justified. 2. On 8 May 2026, the Commission adopted Guidance (1) clarifying that fuel shortages may constitute grounds for the ‘Justified Non-use of Slots’ exception and calling on EU slot-coordinators to adopt a harmonised approach. It also clarified that high kerosene prices cannot constitute grounds for justified non-use of slots under the Slot Regulatio n (2). If the price increases lead to a significant drop in demand, slot relief measures could be considered, as has been the case in previous crises. 3. The interpretative guidelines (3) on Article 5 of the ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation (4) clarify how aircraft operators can be exempted from their refuelling obligation in cases of fuel shortage. The conflict in the Middle East reinforces the need to accelerate the transition towards more diversified energy sources. Maintaining the ambition of ReFuelEU Aviatio n (5) and implementing the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) (6) are therefore essential to strengthen Europe’s energy security, strategic autonomy and competitiveness. If the situation worsens and existing flexibilities no longer suffice, the Commission will propose temporary changes to the applicable EU legislative framework, where justified.
